Ablation and selected Y90 radiation segmentectomy can both have curative intent. Choose by tumor size, location, liver reserve, achievable ablation margin or segmental dosimetry. Ablation has more randomized comparative evidence. Y90 versus ablation studies are mainly observational. Y90 is associated with less waitlist dropout than TACE in registry analyses, but no dedicated randomized comparison establishes a transplant or survival advantage.

H-policy

Later-line efficacy does not define persistent unresectability. HPB MDT must document why complete clearance of every original disease site cannot be achieved with a credible resection/ablation strategy, liver reserve and staged options. Treated/nonviable lesions alone are not proof of active unresectable disease. Preserve all biology, extrahepatic and allocation gates.
Review whether response permits complete treatment of liver disease by resection or ablation; assess the primary and any extrahepatic disease separately.
Medical oncology should review the molecular profile, prior regimens, response, toxicity and performance status to choose systemic treatment or a clinical trial.
After treatment, reassess resectability and disease control. Reconsider transplantation only if the program accepts the full clinical and MELD-exception evidence.
When further tumor-directed therapy is unsuitable or declined, arrange best supportive care, including management of pain, obstruction and other symptoms.

Supported only indirectly — BSG 2023 attributes the better-than-expected survival of the ABC-06 active-symptom-control arm to proactive treatment of biliary obstruction and infection.","refs":["37770126","33798493"]},{"t":"The tumour board operating model, and the standing rule that trial eligibility is checked at diagnosis and at each progression.","why":"These are stakeholder-derived operating requirements, reproduced unchanged across every disease roadmap so the programme has one operating standard rather than five: submission form, triage, stable agenda, urgent referrals, required attendance, imaging reviewed rather than described, pathology pre-alerted, one recommendation with one owner and one reassessment date, documentation within one business day, registry closure. All are evidence grade D by construction — local policy choices with no comparative outcome evidence — and are labelled Standard because the programme has chosen them, not because trials support them. The eligibility rule is defensible in a disease where most of the molecularly matched evidence is single-arm, but no study shows that systematic eligibility checking improves outcome. Everything else, including the liver-function limits for ablation and for ablative radiotherapy, is convention. Unresolved approval item 6, audited through decompensation after liver-directed therapy. The order itself carries no claim either. No randomised trial compares any two of hepatic arterial infusion, radioembolisation, chemoembolisation, ablative radiotherapy and thermal ablation in this disease, and none has been tested against a modern systemic backbone, so the sequence on the page reproduces the roadmap's table and the depth of each dataset rather than a hierarchy of evidence. Unresolved approval item 5. What cannot honestly be given alongside it is an expected outcome. The published 5-year figures in iCCA span 25–73% overall survival and 29–82% recurrence-free survival, almost entirely from single-centre retrospective series, a range the ILTS-ILCA panel itself calls too wide to support a selection rule; almost every series describes iCCA found incidentally or misdiagnosed as hepatocellular carcinoma, so none is an intention-to-treat result and waitlist dropout for progression is unmeasured. Intrahepatic patients were 84 of 447 (19%) and the trial was not powered for site-specific effects, so no iCCA-specific benefit has been shown. The two guideline readings of that subgroup contradict each other — LCSGJ 2022 reports no significant benefit, EASL-ILCA cites a hazard ratio of 0.65 as the best of the subtypes — and they are not two datasets but two readings of one unpowered subgroup of a negative trial. What is actually known is that recurrence was deferred rather than prevented (no difference in recurrence-free survival from 24 to 60 months) and that 44% of treated patients had a grade 3 event, 32% stopped for toxicity and 55% finished all eight cycles. ACTICCA-1 has not reported. Our label is Reasonable consideration, grade C, and the conversation is the deliverable.","refs":["30922733","35978598","37084797","37770126","nccn"]},{"t":"The 3 cm tumour ceiling for a transplant referral.","why":"No study derived it. TOPAZ-1 was 86% metastatic and KEYNOTE-966 89%, both ECOG 0–1, and the TOPAZ-1 investigators state that the trial says nothing about neoadjuvant, downstaging or peri-transplant use in liver-confined disease — which is exactly where the regimen is now borrowed. The absolute gains in the trials as run are 1.3 and 1.8 months of median survival, TOPAZ-1's proportional-hazards assumption was formally violated and it was reported at a prespecified interim analysis, and KEYNOTE-966 missed its prespecified boundaries for both progression-free survival and response. Grade A remains right for clinical decision 9. The choice between them is not an evidence finding either. There is no randomised comparison; ESMO declares the two interchangeable on an indirect comparison across trials differing in chemotherapy duration (gemcitabine capped at eight cycles in TOPAZ-1, continued to progression in KEYNOTE-966), geography and size, and states that no clinical, biochemical or molecular biomarker favours one. Neither trial found a predictive biomarker: benefit did not track PD-L1 in either, MSI status was missing for about half of TOPAZ-1 and only 10 KEYNOTE-966 patients were MSI-high. Present the choice as toxicity profile, schedule and access.","refs":["38319896","37075781","37084797","39864891"]},{"t":"The matched targeted agents in clinical decision 2, as a group.","why":"ClarIDHy and the subsequently reported first-line FIGHT-302 are randomized trials; neither demonstrated an ITT OS advantage. FIGHT-302 used GemCis rather than a modern chemo-immunotherapy comparator. ClarIDHy met progression-free survival (2.7 versus 1.4 months, hazard ratio 0.37) but final intention-to-treat survival was 10.3 versus 7.5 months, hazard ratio 0.79 (0.56–1.12), p=0.09, with 70% crossover; the crossover-adjusted HR is 0.49 with a corrected bootstrap 95% CI of 0.25–1.24 (October 2026; PMID 42879142), so adjusted OS is also not statistically significant. The initial pemigatinib, futibatinib, zanidatamab and dabrafenib–trametinib approvals rested on single-arm data, and none of those registration studies compared against second-line chemotherapy; first-line FIGHT-302 is a separate randomized update. The pemigatinib investigators explicitly warn against the cross-study comparison with pooled second-line chemotherapy that makes their agent look better, since FGFR2-fusion disease itself carries longer survival from diagnosis. Every one is industry-sponsored with sponsor involvement in design, analysis and writing. What is known is response rate and duration in a selected population; what is not known is survival against the alternative. A related choice sits on the same table: our rows require that HER2, NTRK and RET findings be captured but do not name trastuzumab deruxtecan, entrectinib, larotrectinib or selpercatinib, which ESMO 2024 recommends on level III grade A. The reason to hesitate is assay definition and evidence level rather than availability — ESMO concedes there are no standardised criteria for assessing HER2 status in biliary tract cancer and that no specific test can be recommended, while making two HER2-directed recommendations that depend on that undefined assay, and zanidatamab's own data are reported for biliary tract cancer as a whole with no breakdown by subsite. Alignment worksheet, area 14.","refs":["34554208","32416072","38838500","36652354","41264278","32818466","39864891"]},{"t":"Hepatic arterial infusion as the strongest regional option.","why":"The earlier phase 2 study included 38 treated patients at one institution, selected from 84 screened, with the comparison drawn from historical systemic series; the linked editorial judged the case for locoregional therapy in unresectable cholangiocarcinoma still unsettled without a randomised trial, and the authors themselves called for one. The retrospective comparison that gives 30.8 versus 18.4 months had all HAI patients surgically staged against 42% of a 26-patient comparator of whom only 30% received gemcitabine–cisplatin, so stage migration favours HAI; 44 of its 93 HAI patients came from earlier phase 2 trials, and it reports no pump complication or biliary toxicity rate at all. Conversion to curative-intent resection occurred in 8 of 236 patients (3%). Delivery is harder than the figures suggest: 71% received the expected floxuridine dose over the first 3 months and 47% over the next 6, and grade 4 pump or arterial complications forced withdrawal in 11% of the lead-centre cohort and 30% of the 10-patient confirmatory cohort. The deciding variables for the programme are pump expertise, nursing infrastructure and case volume, not the evidence. Updated evidence: PUMP-2 (PMID 41082695), a three-centre nonrandomized phase II study: 50 pumps placed, 48 patients started HAI, partial response 44%, six-month disease control 84%, resection 5/50 (10%), median OS 22.3 months and three-year OS 31.5%. Wei 2025 (PMID 41172153) has since been read in full; it does not establish equivalence, operative superiority or an adopted staging change. Revised 7 October 2026 (Batch 08) after a full-text read of this page's reference depot: 37 structured abstracts, each carrying the authors' own stated limitations and an independent critique with its sources identified, against which every evidence string on this page was rechecked for the published number, for whether the critique undercuts what the string claims, and for whether the grade still follows. Thirty-three evidence strings changed. Three grades were lowered and the reason is recorded in each note: first-line chemo-immunotherapy in permanently unresectable liver-confined disease from A to B, because TOPAZ-1 and KEYNOTE-966 were 86% and 89% metastatic and say nothing about this population; offering adjuvant capecitabine from B to C, because BILCAP did not meet its intention-to-treat primary endpoint and only 19% of its patients had intrahepatic disease; and sequencing a dedicated biliary specimen at ERCP from B to C, because specimens were submitted non-consecutively, the reference standard allowed clinical and radiographic progression in place of tissue, and all testing was done in the laboratory that developed the assay. The transplant assessment was corrected most: the international explant series is now cited only for what it studied — 15 patients with single tumours of 2 cm or less, diagnosed on explant pathology, with mixed hepatocellular-cholangiocarcinoma excluded and no requirement for disease stability on therapy — and the 3 cm ceiling and the six-month stability period in our criteria are attributed to EASL-ILCA, the OPTN review-board guidance and ILTS-ILCA rather than to that series. The ILTS-ILCA 2024 consensus is published twice and both records are cited (PMID 40014003, Liver Transplantation 2025; PMID 42312290, Liver Cancer 2026); the ESMO 2023 parent guideline (PMID 36372281) is now cited alongside its 2024 interim update, since the update covers only molecular diagnostics and advanced disease and leaves the surgical recommendations to the parent. Every reference the page cites was read in full. Still cited from the source document rather than from a full-text read: NCCN Biliary Tract Cancers v1.2026, OPTN Policy 9 and the OPTN Adult MELD Exceptions for Transplant Oncology guidance (December 2025), the Memorial Hermann roadmap and its alignment worksheet, and the HOPE4LIVER one-year histotripsy update, which in any case enrolled hepatocellular carcinoma and metastases rather than intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma. Built from the Memorial Hermann Intrahepatic Cholangiocarcinoma System Roadmap, Draft v0.6 (4 October 2026, including the 3 October 2026 liver-directed treatment revision), and its companion Guideline alignment worksheet of the same date, which compares the roadmap against AASLD 2023, OPTN 2025 review-board guidance, ESMO 2024 interim update, BSG 2023, LCSGJ 2022, ILTS-ILCA 2024 and NCCN Biliary Tract Cancers v1.2026 across 16 areas. Evidence strings carry the published numbers and the published criticism; where the roadmap's label and the trial's primary endpoint diverge, both are stated and the local approval item is named. No recommendation was removed because its evidence turned out to be weak; the roadmap's position stands and the page now says how well supported it is. The liver-directed therapy matrix is read directly from the shared matrix file and is not reproduced here. This page reproduces a draft pending multidisciplinary approval: it is not active clinical policy, does not replace clinician judgement, and every numeric criterion must be verified against the current source before use. HAI sections updated 15 October 2026 to Batch 09. New studies were checked against indexed abstracts and the published ASCO abstract; new full-text PDFs remain to be acquired.   "lead": "Confirm the diagnosis, describe the number and distribution of liver tumors, stage the disease, and assess resection, systemic treatment, liver-directed therapy, and protocol-based transplantation.",

      "id": "1",

      "req": "all",
      "crit": [
        "Histology consistent with intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma, or a high-suspicion mass accepted for direct resection after multidisciplinary HPB review",
        "Multiphase CT of chest, abdomen and pelvis plus liver MRI with cholangiographic (MRCP) sequences, completed before any stent is placed",
        "Another primary excluded — colonoscopy, age-appropriate breast imaging and a CK7/CK20/CDX2-type panel as indicated",
        "Perihilar and distal cholangiocarcinoma and gallbladder cancer require their own treatment assessment. Mixed HCC-iCCA has a separate combined-tumor roadmap; NLRB transplant guidance groups it with iCCA (see clinical decision 10).",
        "Recorded: tumour number and size, vascular and biliary involvement, nodal status, extrahepatic sites, ECOG, Child-Pugh and bilirubin, CA 19-9 and CEA, hepatitis serology"
      ],
      "ask": "Is the diagnosis established, and have all liver lesions, lymph nodes, and distant sites been assessed?",
      "standard": [
        {
          "t": "There is no imaging-only diagnosis of intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma: unlike hepatocellular carcinoma, where LR-5 imaging in an at-risk population is diagnostic, histologic confirmation is required before systemic therapy or a tissue-defined transplant assessment; selected clearly resectable masses may proceed directly to surgery after multidisciplinary review.",
          "l": "Standard",
          "g": "B",
          "refs": [
            "nccn",
            "36083140",
            "37770126",
            "37084797",
            "mhroadmap"
          ],
          "pref": "Every patient whose next step is systemic therapy, trial entry or tissue-defined transplant assessment — in those destinations the tissue criteria are not optional, and transplant assessment additionally needs the biopsy to grade differentiation and to exclude a mixed hepatocellular-cholangiocarcinoma.",
          "avoid": "Do not demand a core from a high-suspicion, clearly resectable mass as a universal rule. NCCN states a suspicious mass on imaging in the proper clinical setting should be treated as malignant, and multidisciplinary HPB review may permit direct resection; the roadmap replaces universal pre-treatment biopsy with destination-specific confirmation.",
          "note": "AASLD 2023 and BSG 2023 require histological confirmation and LCSGJ 2022 regards biopsy as basically unnecessary for a typical resectable mass, so whether a core stays mandatory before resection is a local approval item (alignment worksheet, area 1). CEA and CA 19-9 are baseline and monitoring tests and never establish the diagnosis; CA 19-9 rises with biliary obstruction or cholangitis, so record it alongside the bilirubin and repeat it once the obstruction is relieved."
        },
        {
          "t": "Complete staging and biliary imaging before non-emergency instrumentation. Measure the future liver remnant when major hepatectomy is being considered.",
          "l": "Standard",
          "g": "B",
          "refs": [
            "nccn",
            "37770126",
            "37084797"
          ],
          "pref": "Any patient with a tumour obstructing the biliary tree who might be resected — reactive change from a stent obscures ductal extent, which is exactly what decides whether biliary resection and reconstruction are needed. MRI is the study that characterises the biliary and vascular relationships that determine resectability, and EASL-ILCA prefers it over CT for intrahepatic staging.",
          "avoid": "Do not wait for imaging in cholangitis — that is drained without waiting for the discussion, and urgent sepsis treatment takes priority over the elective sequence.",
          "note": "Where the tumour obstructs the biliary tree, the need for drainage, its route and its side are decided with the hepatobiliary surgeon before any non-emergency procedure; resection without preoperative drainage can be considered when the future remnant is large. That drainage rule is grade D on its own — no comparative outcome data in intrahepatic disease were identified for it — while the grade B on this string covers the imaging sequence, which BSG 2023 and EASL-ILCA both recommend."
        },
        {
          "t": "Exclude another primary before committing to this pathway, because metastatic adenocarcinoma can be histologically indistinguishable from intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma.",
          "l": "Standard",
          "g": "D",
          "refs": [
            "mhroadmap"
          ],
          "pref": "Any adenocarcinoma in the liver without an established primary, and particularly before a patient is started on a biliary-tract regimen or entered into a biliary trial.",
          "avoid": "Do not let the immunohistochemical panel consume the whole core: BSG 2023 asks that tissue be reserved for molecular profiling when immunohistochemistry is planned, and whether to add that instruction is a local approval item (alignment worksheet, area 12).",
          "note": "Treating a colorectal or pancreatic metastasis as intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma is a recognised and consequential error. Hepatitis B and C status and any cirrhosis are established at entry: they change operative risk and, where a mixed tumour is possible, the differential."

        {
          "t": "Describe every suspected tumor nodule by number, size, liver segment, and relationship to the main tumor. Distinguish liver-confined multifocal disease from regional nodal involvement and distant metastases.",
          "l": "Standard",
          "g": "D",
          "refs": [
            "capicca",
            "rcpafocality",
            "41172153"

          "avoid": "Do not label all additional liver nodules as distant stage IV disease, assume satellites are harmless, or infer independent primary tumors from imaging alone.",
          "note": "The descriptions overlap biologically. Record imaging uncertainty and obtain expert radiology/pathology review rather than assigning a treatment solely from the label."
        }
      ],
      "alt": [
        {
          "t": "Plan molecular testing of a dedicated biliary specimen at the index ERCP where the disease presents as an indeterminate stricture rather than a mass and the alternative is a repeat procedure.",
          "l": "Reasonable",
          "g": "C",
          "refs": [
            "41905432",
            "30971436"
          ],
          "pref": "The patient entering the pathway as an indeterminate stricture, where pathology alone is weakest: in a 6-year prospective study of 2,116 patients across 28 institutions, pathologic assessment of ERCP brushings and biopsies had 44% sensitivity overall and 36% for intrahepatic or hilar strictures, while a DNA/RNA sequencing panel on separately collected specimens in a dedicated nucleic-acid buffer reached 82% sensitivity at 98% specificity and the combination 88% at 97%. Specificity was 99% for pathology, so sequencing bought sensitivity and gave up almost nothing.",
          "avoid": "Do not read a negative molecular result as excluding malignancy — in the original single-centre cohort there were 37 false negatives (25%) and the negative predictive value was only 63%, with sampling failure the usual explanation; in 12 of those cases the same panel found an alteration in the resected tumour. Only 2% of neoplastic strictures in the 2026 study were purely dysplastic, so outside primary sclerosing cholangitis this is earlier diagnosis of established cancer, not early detection, and no resectability or survival benefit has been shown. Payer authorisation and the dedicated collection buffer have to be arranged before the procedure, not after.",
          "note": "Correct the yield figure: therapeutically relevant alterations were reported in 20 of 150 cancers (13%) in the original single-centre cohort, and in the 2026 multi-institutional study in 137 of 458 cholangiocarcinomas (30%) — but only on the 161-gene version of the panel.         },
        {
          "t": "Add FDG-PET selectively, for suspected occult spread and for transplant staging.",
          "l": "Reasonable",
          "g": "B",
          "refs": [
            "nccn",
            "37770126",
            "37084797"
          ],
          "pref": "Where occult nodal or distant disease would change the operation, and in any patient being staged for a transplant protocol.",

          "note": "BSG 2023 recommends FDG-PET-CT for nodal and distant disease as part of staging and EASL-ILCA recommends it routinely in apparently resectable patients, both more broadly than our selective wording — alignment worksheet, area 2.           "g": "D",

            "37770126"

          "g": "D",
          "refs": [

          "pref": "Use the separate perihilar roadmap; gallbladder cancer, mixed hepatocellular-cholangiocarcinoma and paediatric disease are out of scope here.",
          "avoid": "In particular, the standardised perihilar MELD exception and its neoadjuvant/stricture protocol do not transfer to intrahepatic disease."
        }
      ]

  "provenance": "Website language revised 23 October 2026 to use direct clinical questions and consistent terminology. The focality clarification additionally uses CAP intrahepatic bile-duct protocol v4.3 (June 2025), EASL–ILCA 2023 and current OPTN NLRB guidance. Wei 2025 (PMID 41172153) has since been read in full; it does not establish equivalence, operative superiority or an adopted staging change. Revised 7 October 2026 (Batch 08) after a full-text read of this page's reference depot: 37 structured abstracts, each carrying the authors' own stated limitations and an independent critique with its sources identified, against which every evidence string on this page was rechecked for the published number, for whether the critique undercuts what the string claims, and for whether the grade still follows. Thirty-three evidence strings changed. Three grades were lowered and the reason is recorded in each note: first-line chemo-immunotherapy in permanently unresectable liver-confined disease from A to B, because TOPAZ-1 and KEYNOTE-966 were 86% and 89% metastatic and say nothing about this population; offering adjuvant capecitabine from B to C, because BILCAP did not meet its intention-to-treat primary endpoint and only 19% of its patients had intrahepatic disease; and sequencing a dedicated biliary specimen at ERCP from B to C, because specimens were submitted non-consecutively, the reference standard allowed clinical and radiographic progression in place of tissue, and all testing was done in the laboratory that developed the assay. The transplant assessment was corrected most: the international explant series is now cited only for what it studied — 15 patients with single tumours of 2 cm or less, diagnosed on explant pathology, with mixed hepatocellular-cholangiocarcinoma excluded and no requirement for disease stability on therapy — and the 3 cm ceiling and the six-month stability period in our criteria are attributed to EASL-ILCA, the OPTN review-board guidance and ILTS-ILCA rather than to that series. The ILTS-ILCA 2024 consensus is published twice and both records are cited (PMID 40014003, Liver Transplantation 2025; PMID 42312290, Liver Cancer 2026); the ESMO 2023 parent guideline (PMID 36372281) is now cited alongside its 2024 interim update, since the update covers only molecular diagnostics and advanced disease and leaves the surgical recommendations to the parent. Every reference the page cites was read in full. Still cited from the source document rather than from a full-text read: NCCN Biliary Tract Cancers v1.2026, OPTN Policy 9 and the OPTN Adult MELD Exceptions for Transplant Oncology guidance (December 2025), the Memorial Hermann roadmap and its alignment worksheet, and the HOPE4LIVER one-year histotripsy update, which in any case enrolled hepatocellular carcinoma and metastases rather than intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma. Built from the Memorial Hermann Intrahepatic Cholangiocarcinoma System Roadmap, Draft v0.6 (4 October 2026, including the 3 October 2026 liver-directed treatment revision), and its companion Guideline alignment worksheet of the same date, which compares the roadmap against AASLD 2023, OPTN 2025 review-board guidance, ESMO 2024 interim update, BSG 2023, LCSGJ 2022, ILTS-ILCA 2024 and NCCN Biliary Tract Cancers v1.2026 across 16 areas. Evidence strings carry the published numbers and the published criticism; where the roadmap's label and the trial's primary endpoint diverge, both are stated and the local approval item is named. No recommendation was removed because its evidence turned out to be weak; the roadmap's position stands and the page now says how well supported it is. The liver-directed therapy matrix is read directly from the shared matrix file and is not reproduced here. This page reproduces a draft pending multidisciplinary approval: it is not active clinical policy, does not replace clinician judgement, and every numeric criterion must be verified against the current source before use. HAI sections updated 15 October 2026 to Batch 09. New studies were checked against indexed abstracts and the published ASCO abstract; new full-text PDFs remain to be acquired. No new full-text review is claimed for these additions."

  "provenance": "Built from the Memorial Hermann Colorectal Liver Metastasis System Roadmap Draft v0.6 (4 October 2026, liver-directed section revised 3 October 2026, evidence current to 20 September 2026) and its companion guideline alignment worksheet of the same date, which supplied the institutional positions, the NCCN decisions 1-16 and the open local approval items. Revised on 7 October 2026 (Batch 08) after a full-text read of the whole CRLM reference depot: 45 papers, each with an independently recorded critique, covering all 45 PubMed-indexed references cited on this page. Every evidence string was re-checked against the paper's own reported results rather than against a guideline quoting it, and the grades were re-set where the full text showed the recommendation rested on a surrogate endpoint, a subset analysis, an unvalidated threshold or a single centre's practice; 20 evidence entries changed and 13 grades were lowered in that pass, and the limited-evidence section was rewritten and expanded from 5 entries to 27. Three references are cited only for what they do not yet show: the older PUMP protocol is now supplemented by the ASCO 2026 randomized abstract; the LIGRO survival analysis is published separately and was not read, so ALPPS is cited for resectability only; and the NCCN guideline, the OPTN policy and guidance documents, the Memorial Hermann roadmap and its alignment worksheet are not PubMed-indexed papers and were read as documents, not trials. Policy wording follows NCCN Colon Cancer v2.2026 (7 April 2026), OPTN Policy 9 as retrieved 1 October 2026, and the OPTN Adult MELD Exceptions for Transplant Oncology review-board guidance of December 2025, which is guidance and not Policy. The roadmap itself is a draft pending multidisciplinary and institutional governance review: it is not active clinical policy, does not replace clinician judgement, current drug labelling, OPTN policy or patient-specific informed consent, and every transplant criterion must be confirmed against current policy at implementation. HAI sections updated 15 October 2026 to Batch 09. New studies were checked against indexed abstracts and the published ASCO abstract; new full-text PDFs remain to be acquired. No new full-text review is claimed for these additions."
}

The decision points follow the roadmap's own sequence: §2 (its clinical decision 0, drainage), §3 (define the extent), §4 and §4.1 (tissue and route), §5 (its clinical decision 1, resectable disease), §6 (its clinical decision 2, the transplant protocol), and §7 (its Decision points 3 and 4). {
  "key": "nelm",
  "short": "NELM",
  "name": "Neuroendocrine liver metastases",
  "version": "v0.7",
  "batch": "Batch 08, 7 October 2026",
  "lead": "Use tumor differentiation, grade, disease distribution, symptoms, and liver function to select treatment for neuroendocrine liver metastases.",
  "gatelabel": "Clinical decisions",
  "gates": [
    {
      "id": "1",
      "tone": "cure",
      "name": "1 · Confirm differentiation and grade",
      "req": "all",
      "crit": [
        "Biopsy reporting differentiation and a representative Ki-67 index; include a mitotic count when evaluable. Document tissue adequacy and resolve discordance with expert pathology review.",
        "Somatostatin-receptor PET/CT for receptor status and whole-body staging",
        "Functional syndrome recorded explicitly, confirmed with directed tests",
        "Hepatic burden and distribution: unilobar versus bilobar, resectable versus diffuse-miliary",
        "Primary site, whether it is resected, and the extrahepatic sites"
      ],
      "ask": "Is the tumor a well-differentiated NET or a poorly differentiated neuroendocrine carcinoma, and what are its grade and Ki-67 index?",
      "standard": [
        {
          "t": "Obtain expert pathology reporting differentiation and representative Ki-67, with mitoses when evaluable. An adequate small biopsy may be graded with Ki-67 when mitoses cannot be assessed; inadequate or discordant tissue needs review and further sampling if it would change treatment.",
          "l": "Standard",
          "g": "C",
          "refs": [
            "28609356",
            "36924180"
          ],
          "pref": "Every patient before a pathway is assigned, and again on any specimen sampled metachronously — a well-differentiated G3 tumour and a poorly differentiated carcinoma can share a Ki-67 range and need different pathways.",
          "avoid": "Do not accept a report giving Ki-67 as a range, and do not let grade stand in for differentiation; if the report does not say which it is, ask the pathologist before the board meets.",
          "note": "Downgraded to C on the full-text read. The requirement is right but its evidence is consensus, not comparison: NANETS 2017 means a show of hands from a 15-member panel with no evidence grading and no systematic literature search, and consensus was recorded only that both differentiation and grade be reported, with a significant majority — 75% or more — that both mitotic rate and Ki-67 be measured and fine-needle aspiration accepted as adequate in most cases. ENETS 2023 explicitly states that Ki-67 alone cannot distinguish NET G3 from NEC. Use differentiation, morphology and appropriate immunohistochemistry; 55% is not a diagnostic boundary. A mixed neuroendocrine–non-neuroendocrine neoplasm is named as such, and its clinically dominant aggressive component sets the pathway."
        },
        {
          "t": "Stage with somatostatin-receptor PET/CT, 68Ga-DOTATATE or equivalent, alongside cross-sectional CT or MRI.",
          "l": "Standard",
          "g": "B",
          "refs": [
            "33588146",
            "37774329"
          ],
          "pref": "Use SSTR imaging for staging and when it will change management, including PRRT assessment or discordant progression. Use CT/MRI for routine response surveillance and repeat receptor imaging selectively.",
          "avoid": "Do not use receptor uptake as a substitute for anatomic burden assessment or as a universal response measure, and do not order octreotide SPECT/CT unless SSTR-PET is unavailable.",
          "note": "Graded B on diagnostic accuracy rather than on outcome: NANETS 2017 reports 68Ga-DOTATATE PET/CT sensitivity of 95% against 31% for octreotide SPECT, which is why the substitution is made. The EANM position itself is a modified three-round Delphi vote — necessary at staging of all NET in 19 of 23 panellists (82.6%), CT or MRI also necessary in 20 of 23 (87.0%) — with consensus set at 70% agreement for a single answer and only 50% preference in multiple-choice format, and consensus failed on 12 of 43 questions. The panel was drawn from high-volume centres with full access to Ga-68 tracer and PRRT, so availability is assumed rather than tested. Where SSTR-PET has not been done, the board records its absence explicitly rather than proceeding as if it had."
        },
        {
          "t": "Record carcinoid syndrome, insulinoma, gastrinoma or any other functional syndrome explicitly, confirmed with tests directed at the suspected syndrome rather than a panel of every available marker.",
          "l": "Standard",
          "g": "D",
          "refs": [
            "39266864"
          ],
          "pref": "Before any hepatic procedure — this changes procedural safety planning, not only symptom management, and high hepatic burden with a midgut primary is the dominant carcinoid-crisis risk combination.",
          "avoid": "Do not treat a normal marker panel as excluding a functional syndrome, and do not leave the syndrome undocumented because symptoms are currently controlled on an analogue.",
          "note": "Grade D: a named local requirement with no comparative outcome evidence behind the thresholds themselves."
        },
        {
          "t": "State the hepatic tumour burden, unilobar versus bilobar, resectable versus diffuse-miliary pattern, the primary site and whether it is resected, the extrahepatic sites, and which problem is driving the clinical picture.",
          "l": "Standard",
          "g": "D",
          "pref": "Every case at submission: burden and distribution decide whether cytoreduction, embolotherapy or transplantation is an option at all.",
          "avoid": "Do not open a treatment discussion where the dominant problem has not been named — hormonal symptoms and tumour progression need different answers and conflating them produces treatment without an endpoint."
        }
      ],
      "alt": [
        {
          "t": "Obtain FDG PET where the grade is high, where behaviour is discordant with grade, where SSTR uptake is heterogeneous, or where a CT or MRI lesion shows no SSTR uptake.",
          "l": "Reasonable",
          "g": "B",
          "refs": [
            "33588146",
            "39395114"
          ],
          "pref": "Before committing to receptor-directed therapy in G2–G3 disease or rapid progression, to find receptor-negative, FDG-avid disease that PRRT will not treat.",
          "avoid": "Not for routine staging of well-differentiated disease, where NANETS found no value in it.",
          "note": "The roadmap keeps FDG selective on the Itanet triggers rather than requiring it for every G2–G3 PRRT candidate as EANM Focus 3 does. EANM endorsed FDG before PRRT in G2–G3 to exclude mismatched FDG-positive, SSTR-negative lesions in 19 of 23 panellists (82.6%) by modified Delphi, and Itanet grades the FDG trigger 3b-A. What neither establishes is that acting on the mismatch changes outcome: EANM's extension of PRRT into G3 rests on two small retrospective series confined to Ki-67 under 55%, and EANM reached no consensus at all on PRRT with mismatched lesions."
        },
        {
          "t": "Consider re-biopsy on unexpected behavioural change or discordant FDG avidity.",
          "l": "Reasonable",
          "g": "C",
          "refs": [
            "39395114"
          ],
          "pref": "Where the original grading is years old or the disease has clearly changed pace: grade progression and transformation both occur and change the pathway.",
          "avoid": "Not as a scheduled ritual — no study defines the trigger or the interval, which is why this sits at C and remains an open local decision.",
          "note": "Itanet attaches 3a-A to re-evaluation before radioligand therapy when behaviour changes, which is stronger than the roadmap's 'consider'; whether it becomes a required step before PRRT is a local approval item."
        }
      ],
      "avoid": [
        {
          "t": "Do not assign a pathway on grade alone.",
          "l": "Avoid",
          "g": "D",
          "pref": "The differentiation fork drives every later decision, so the tissue standard is deliberately set high.",
          "avoid": "If differentiation cannot be established on the available material, get more material rather than guessing from Ki-67."
        },
        {
          "t": "Do not manage a poorly differentiated carcinoma on the indolent-disease pathway.",
          "l": "Avoid",
          "g": "B",
          "refs": [
            "36924180"

  "provenance": "Built from the Memorial Hermann Neuroendocrine Liver Metastasis System Roadmap, Draft v0.6 dated 4 October 2026 with its liver-directed therapy section revised 3 October 2026, and from the companion guideline alignment worksheet of the same date, which compares the roadmap against NCCN Neuroendocrine and Adrenal Tumors v1.2026 (21 April 2026), NANETS 2017 medical and surgical consensus statements, NANETS 2020 surgical consensus, EANM Focus 3 (2021), Itanet 2024, ENETS 2023–2024 guidance and the OPTN National Liver Review Board transplant-oncology guidance of December 2025 against OPTN Policy 9 as checked on 1 October 2026. Revised on 7 October 2026 (Batch 08) after a full-text read of the whole NELM reference depot: 33 papers, each carrying an independently recorded critique, covering all 33 PubMed-indexed references cited on this page. Every evidence string was re-checked against each paper's own reported results rather than against a guideline quoting it, and grades were re-set where the full text showed a recommendation resting on a surrogate endpoint, a cohort with no comparator arm, an unvalidated threshold or a consensus vote; 40 evidence strings changed and 4 grades were lowered in that pass, and the limited-evidence section was rewritten and expanded from 9 entries to 34 with six further local approval items added. Four references are cited partly or wholly for what they do not show: RETNET (PMID 30016989) is a published protocol with no outcome data, so no efficacy figure on this page rests on it and the drug-eluting-bead arm closure is attributed to the ENETS 2024 guidance that reports it; the ENETS 2023 digestive neuroendocrine carcinoma paper is cited for a recommendation it grades 5D; NANETS 2017 medical and NANETS 2020 surgical are cited in several places for recorded absences of consensus. One figure on the page is cited from a guideline rather than from the paper itself and was not read in full: the Maire 2012 randomised TAE versus TACE trial of 26 patients, quoted from ENETS. The NCCN guideline, the OPTN policy and review-board guidance, the HOPE4LIVER update, the Memorial Hermann roadmap and its alignment worksheet are not PubMed-indexed depot papers and were read as documents; the ASCO 2025 symptom-management guideline is PubMed-indexed (PMID 40344544) but was outside the depot and was read as a document. The liver-directed therapy matrix is rendered from the shared modality matrix, which is outside this page's scope and which carries RETNET outcome figures the protocol paper does not report; approval item 12 assigns its correction. Both source documents are drafts pending multidisciplinary and institutional governance review: they are not active clinical policy, do not replace clinician judgement, current drug labelling, OPTN policy or patient-specific informed consent, and every numeric criterion must be verified against its current source before use."

ENETS 2023 explicitly states that Ki-67 alone cannot distinguish NET G3 from NEC. Use differentiation, morphology and appropriate immunohistochemistry; 55% is not a diagnostic boundary.   "provenance": "Built from the Memorial Hermann Neuroendocrine Liver Metastasis System Roadmap, Draft v0.6 dated 4 October 2026 with its liver-directed therapy section revised 3 October 2026, and from the companion guideline alignment worksheet of the same date, which compares the roadmap against NCCN Neuroendocrine and Adrenal Tumors v1.2026 (21 April 2026), NANETS 2017 medical and surgical consensus statements, NANETS 2020 surgical consensus, EANM Focus 3 (2021), Itanet 2024, ENETS 2023–2024 guidance and the OPTN National Liver Review Board transplant-oncology guidance of December 2025 against OPTN Policy 9 as checked on 1 October 2026. Revised on 7 October 2026 (Batch 08) after a full-text read of the whole NELM reference depot: 33 papers, each carrying an independently recorded critique, covering all 33 PubMed-indexed references cited on this page. Every evidence string was re-checked against each paper's own reported results rather than against a guideline quoting it, and grades were re-set where the full text showed a recommendation resting on a surrogate endpoint, a cohort with no comparator arm, an unvalidated threshold or a consensus vote; 40 evidence strings changed and 4 grades were lowered in that pass, and the limited-evidence section was rewritten and expanded from 9 entries to 34 with six further local approval items added. Four references are cited partly or wholly for what they do not show: RETNET (PMID 30016989) is a published protocol with no outcome data, so no efficacy figure on this page rests on it and the drug-eluting-bead arm closure is attributed to the ENETS 2024 guidance that reports it; the ENETS 2023 digestive neuroendocrine carcinoma paper is cited for a recommendation it grades 5D; NANETS 2017 medical and NANETS 2020 surgical are cited in several places for recorded absences of consensus. One figure on the page is cited from a guideline rather than from the paper itself and was not read in full: the Maire 2012 randomised TAE versus TACE trial of 26 patients, quoted from ENETS. The liver-directed therapy matrix is rendered from the shared modality matrix, which is outside this page's scope and which carries RETNET outcome figures the protocol paper does not report; approval item 12 assigns its correction.
